focus: Stress on the surviving auxiliary: 'So DO I' · 'Neither HAVE they' · 'one/ones' substitution · 'do so' and 'do the same' · what stress remains after ellipsis
focus_ar: النبر على الفعل المساعد الباقي: 'So DO I'، و'Neither HAVE they'، والاستبدال بـ 'one/ones'، و'do so' و'do the same'، والنبر الباقي بعد الحذف
arabic_challenge: Ellipsis removes words, and the ones that survive absorb all the stress. In 'So do I', 'do' replaces an entire verb phrase, so it must be strong — 'So DO I'. Learners often say it flatly, which sounds oddly uncommitted, or they avoid ellipsis altogether and repeat the full verb, which sounds laboured. Arabic agreement patterns allow repetition without awkwardness (وأنا أيضًا أحبّ ذلك), so there is no pressure to compress. The skill here is trusting that a single strong auxiliary can carry a whole clause.

target_sounds: 'So DO I' — stress on the substituting auxiliary

isolation.instructions: 'So do I' means 'I do too'. Because 'do' stands in for the whole verb phrase, it takes the stress: 'So DO I'. Note the inversion — auxiliary before subject. Match the auxiliary to the original verb: 'I can' gives 'So CAN I'.
isolation.instructions_ar: 'So do I' تعني 'وأنا أيضًا'. لأن 'do' تنوب عن العبارة الفعلية كلها فهي تأخذ النبر، مع قلب المساعد قبل الفاعل.

sentence_practice: I love this city. — So do I.
We've already finished. — So have we.
daily_drills.record_this: I genuinely love this city, and apparently so does everyone who visits it. She was completely exhausted by the end of the week, and so was I. We have already finished our section, and so have the other two teams.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'So do I'. Is 'do' clearly the strongest word, with the auxiliary before the subject?

target_sounds: 'Neither HAVE they' · 'Nor DO I' — negative agreement

isolation.instructions: For negative agreement use 'neither' or 'nor', and again the auxiliary is strong: 'Neither HAVE they', 'Nor DO I'. The verb after it stays positive — the negativity lives in 'neither/nor'. 'Neither' is /ˈnaɪðə/ or /ˈniːðə/; both are correct.
isolation.instructions_ar: للموافقة في النفي استخدم 'neither' أو 'nor'، والمساعد يبقى قويًا، والفعل بعده مثبت لأن النفي في 'neither/nor'.

sentence_practice: I don't agree. — Neither do I.
They haven't replied. — Nor have we.
She didn't understand, and nor did I.
daily_drills.record_this: I don't agree with the conclusion at all, and neither does my colleague. They still haven't replied to the original message, and nor have we. She clearly didn't understand the question, and nor did I, if I'm honest.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'Neither do I'. Is the auxiliary strong, and did you avoid a double negative?

isolation.instructions: 'one/ones' replaces a repeated noun. The substitute itself is usually weak; the describing word takes the stress: 'the RED one', 'the CHEAPER ones'. Saying 'the red ONE' shifts the emphasis oddly onto the substitute, which sounds unnatural.
isolation.instructions_ar: 'one/ones' تنوب عن الاسم المتكرّر، والبديل نفسه خفيف عادةً والصفة تأخذ النبر. نبر البديل يبدو غير طبيعي.

sentence_practice: I'll take the cheaper ones, thanks.
The ones we ordered never arrived.
daily_drills.record_this: I think I'll take the cheaper ones, if that's genuinely all right with you. Which one of the two proposals did you actually prefer in the end? The ones we ordered back in March never arrived at all.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'the cheaper ones'. Is 'cheaper' stressed and 'ones' light?

target_sounds: 'do so' · 'do the same' — formal verb substitution

isolation.instructions: 'do so' replaces a whole verb phrase in formal English: 'She was asked to explain, and she did so willingly.' 'Do' is light here and 'so' takes a small beat. 'Do the same' is the everyday equivalent, with the beat on SAME.
isolation.instructions_ar: 'do so' تنوب عن عبارة فعلية كاملة في الإنجليزية الرسمية، و'do' خفيفة و'so' تأخذ نبضة صغيرة، و'do the same' هي المكافئ اليومي.

sentence_practice: She was asked to explain and did so willingly.
Anyone wishing to object may do so in writing.
He apologised, and I did the same.
daily_drills.record_this: She was asked to explain her reasoning and did so willingly and in detail. Anyone wishing to object to the proposal may do so in writing before Friday. He apologised properly at the end, and I did the same.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'and did so willingly'. Is 'do' light, with a small beat on 'so'?

target_sounds: ellipsis proper: what survives takes the weight

isolation.instructions: English routinely deletes repeated material: 'I'd like to come but I can't [come].' Whatever survives at the end of the clause takes a strong, final beat, often with a small fall: 'but I CAN'T ↘'. The deleted words leave their stress behind on the remaining auxiliary.
isolation.instructions_ar: الإنجليزية تحذف المُعاد كثيرًا، وما يبقى في نهاية الجملة يأخذ نبضة قوية نهائية مع هبوط صغير.
practice: I'd like to but I CAN'T ↘
She said she would, and she DID ↘

pair: she said she would, and she DID
she said she would come, and she came
I haven't finished, but he has finished
if you want to do it

sentence_practice: I'd like to come, but I can't.
She said she would help, and she did.
I haven't finished, but he has.
daily_drills.record_this: I would genuinely like to come along tomorrow, but unfortunately I can't. She said she would help us with the final section, and she absolutely did. I haven't finished my part of the report yet, but he has.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'I'd like to come, but I can't'. Does 'can't' take a strong final beat with a small fall?

challenge_sentences: I agree completely. — So do I.
They never replied, and nor did we.
I'll take the smaller ones, please.
She promised to call, and she did.
daily_drills.record_this: I agree completely with what you said, and so does almost everyone here. They never replied to our letter, and nor did we chase it up properly. I think I'll take the smaller ones instead, if that's possible. She promised to call before the weekend, and she did.
daily_drills.self_check: Three checks: strong substituting auxiliary, no double negative after 'neither', and a strong final beat on whatever survives ellipsis.

test_yourself.instructions: Record yourself reading this as a natural conversation with yourself as both speakers. Ellipsis is the rhythm of real dialogue, so keep it quick — then listen back and check.
test_yourself.instructions_ar: سجّل نفسك تقرأ هذا كمحادثة طبيعية بدورين. الحذف هو إيقاع الحوار الحقيقي، فاجعله سريعًا، ثم اسمع وراجع.
test_yourself.passage: I thought the meeting went reasonably well, and apparently so did everyone else. Rashid wasn't convinced, though, and neither was Layla. They had both read the earlier draft; I hadn't, which probably explains why I was less critical. When the chair asked for written objections, two people said they would submit them, and one actually did so. The others didn't. I'd have preferred a clearer decision, but we didn't get one. Someone suggested reordering the agenda, and I wish we had. The longer items should have come first; the shorter ones could easily have waited. If anyone wants to raise it again next week, they can, and I suspect somebody will. I'd support them if they did. So would Rashid, I think, though he hasn't said so directly.

sounds_to_check.strong substituting auxiliary: apparently so DID everyone else · neither WAS Layla · So WOULD Rashid
sounds_to_check.negative agreement without double negati: and neither was Layla · The others didn't
sounds_to_check.'one/ones' with the describer stressed: we didn't get ONE · the LONGER items · the SHORTER ones
sounds_to_check.'do so' formal substitution: one actually did so · he hasn't said so directly
sounds_to_check.ellipsis with a strong final beat: I HADN'T ↘ · but we DIDN'T ↘ · they CAN ↘ · I suspect somebody WILL ↘

scoring_guide.90_100: Substituting auxiliaries strong, no double negatives, ellipsis landing on a clear final beat. Sounds genuinely conversational. Ready for week 12.
scoring_guide.70_89: Good; occasionally an auxiliary goes flat or a full verb is repeated unnecessarily.
scoring_guide.50_69: Ellipsis avoided or delivered flatly, so speech sounds laboured. Repeat days 1-2 and day 5.
scoring_guide.below_50: Redo days 1-5. Start with 'So DO I' until the strong auxiliary feels automatic.

for_arabic_speakers: The auxiliary that replaces a verb phrase is ALWAYS stressed: 'So DO I', not 'so do I'.
Invert after 'so' and 'neither': 'So do I', never 'So I do'.
Never add a second negative: 'Neither do I', not 'Neither don't I'.
With 'one/ones' the describing word takes the stress: 'the CHEAPER ones'.
'do so' is formal; 'do it' or 'do the same' is everyday. Choose to match the register you are in.
supplementary_notes.recording_requirement: Record the 'record_this' line daily; on day 7 check that every surviving auxiliary is genuinely strong.
